title: Research Bite #57: Attention Hijacked: How Social Media Notifications Disrupt Cognitive Processing
author: Craig Barton
summary: Research Bite #57 covers Hippolyte Fournier, Arnaud Fournel, François Osiurak, Olivier Koenig, Flora Pâris, Vivien Gaujoux, and Fabien Ringeval's 'Attention hijacked: How social media notifications disrupt cognitive processing,' published in Computers in Human Behavior (2026, Vol. 179). Using a Stroop task interrupted by smartphone-style notifications, the researchers tracked both behavioral reaction times and physiological measures (pupil dilation) in an ecologically valid lab setting with university students averaging 20.6 years old. Notifications produced a measurable slowdown in cognitive processing lasting roughly seven seconds, driven by perceptual salience, learned association, and the notification's inferred relevance -- and the size of that disruption tracked a person's notification-checking frequency and volume, not total screen time. The physiological data (pupil dilation) mirrored the behavioral findings, confirming the effect isn't just a reporting artifact. Barton flags the caveat that the sample was adult university students in a controlled lab, so the exact disruption dynamics in younger students with still-developing attentional systems remain an open question.
points: The finding that disruption severity tracks notification frequency and checking habits -- not total screen time -- reframes 'screen time' as the wrong metric for schools and parents to focus on when addressing phone-related attention problems.

A roughly seven-second reaction-time cost per notification sounds small in isolation, but students receiving 150+ notifications a day accumulates into substantial fragmented-attention exposure across a school day.
Corroborating the behavioral slowdown with pupil-dilation data (a physiological arousal marker) strengthens the claim beyond self-report or simple reaction-time noise.

Because the study used university students (mean age 20.6) in a controlled lab, Barton's own summary flags that younger students with still-developing attentional systems may show different -- possibly more severe -- disruption dynamics, a genuine limit on generalizability.

The 'sensitisation' framing -- habitual smartphone use makes the brain more responsive to digital cues over time -- suggests the problem compounds with exposure rather than staying constant, an argument for earlier rather than later intervention.
quotes: This study investigates how social media notifications act as digital hijackers that disrupt cognitive processing and task performance.
In an ecologically valid experiment, researchers found that alerts cause a temporary slowdown in reaction time, lasting roughly 7 seconds.
This interference is driven by a combination of perceptual salience, learned conditioning, and the personal relevance of the notification.
The severity of this disruption is most accurately predicted by a user's frequency of interaction—specifically, notification volume and checking habits—rather than total screen time.

These behavioural findings were supported by physiological data, as pupil dilation patterns confirmed that more relevant notifications trigger higher levels of arousal. Ultimately, the research suggests that habitual smartphone use sensitises the brain to these digital cues, making them difficult to ignore even when they lack immediate importance.
